Pathophysiology
The progression of HF is similar to that of atherosclerosis be-
cause there is an asymptomatic phase when damage is silently 
occurring (stages A and B) (see Figure 33-11). HF is initiated by 
damage or stress to the heart muscle either of acute MI or in-
sidious (hemodynamic pressure or volume overloading) onset 
(see Table 33-5 for classifications of HF).
The progressive insult alters the function and shape of the 
left ventricle such that it hypertrophies in an effort to sustain 
blood flow, a process known as cardiac remodeling. Symp-
toms do not usually arise until months or years after cardiac 
remodeling begins. Many compensatory mechanisms from 
the SNS, RAS, and cytokine system are activated to restore 
The lifetime risk of developing HF is 20% for Americans 
age 40 or older. Approximately 5.1 million in the United 
States have HF. The incidence increases with age, rising 
from approximately 20 per 1000 individuals 65 to 69 years 
to greater than 80 per 1000 in those individuals 85 and 
older (Stone et al, 2014). Black men have been shown to be at 
the highest risk of HF; white women have the lowest. HF in 
non-Hispanic black males and females has a prevalence of
